newsitem.title: USA: OVERNIGHT- U.S. TREASURIES END HIGHER.
newsitem.headline: OVERNIGHT- U.S. TREASURIES END HIGHER.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices awoke from early slumber and closed mostly higher on Friday, as technical buying took the long end of the market to four-month highs before giving way to late session profit taking.

The 30-year bond closed at 99-18/32, up 9/32, while its yield edged down to 6.66 percent from 6.68 percent. The bond was as high as 99-24/32 and its yield as low as 6.64 percent -- levels not seen since February 21.
"It seems like there is a real need for paper," said Brett Benza, senior trader at Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette Securities.
"I don't know when the need will be satisfied but it is not being satisfied," he said.
Trading was described as very light, evidenced by GovPx volume of just above 50 billion.
"Half of Wall Street was in Westchester watching golf," said one player, referring to this weekend's Buick Open.
Many of those who had to work said market activity was as exciting as like watching paint dry.
As a result, price action was clearly exaggerated, they said. "The market can be pushed around on days like today," Benza said.
As has been the case all week, Treasuries started off slowly on Friday. And with no economic news to speak of, technical factors dominated the session.
Hedge funds and foreign accounts were seen buying, and momentum ahead of the July options expiration helped boost the market.
Then, once the September T-bond broke through a key level at 112-12/32, more buying was triggered.
Players noted that the long end led the front end, sparking a further narrowing of the yield curve.

The spread between the two-year note and 30-year bond narrowed to 65 basis points, the lowest point since May 13. The two-year had made a bid to close below 6.0 percent, but it failed like it has each time the past two weeks.
The two-year note's yield closed at 6.00 percent, breaking below the low of 6.01 percent seen all week. The issue hadn't been so low since closing at 5.90 percent on February 25.
"If we don't start get strong data next week from home sales and durable goods, (the two-year) is going to 5.85 percent," predicted Patrick Dimick, Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities LLC.
The risk, analysts noted, was that the Street may try to build in concessions on Monday ahead of the two- and five-year auctions on Tuesday and Wednesday, respectively.

Also helping the market on Friday was talk a state fund bought at the longer end. Players said there was a rumor that the fund's portfolio weighting in bonds falls when the stock market continues to rally. Some said many states have laws requiring certain portions of their portfolios in bonds.
Numerous traders said they had not heard of such laws. Yet, they added, the talk was enough to add to the market's bullish tone.
"We had an asset squeeze today," Benza said of the market action. "People can't get enough financial assets."
Late in the session some day-traders booked profits, taking the market off its highs.
Five-year notes closed unchanged at 100-29/32 to yield 6.28 percent and the 10-year note was up 3/32 to 101-24/32 to yield 6.38 percent.
Bill rates ended unchanged, with three-month bills at 4.94 percent, six-month bills at 5.08 percent and year bills at 5.34 percent.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
